title: Phase-controlled transport of Floquet-driven compact topological photonic states
authors: Gabriel Caceres-Aravena, Paloma Vildoso, Helena Drüeke, Rodrigo A. Vicencio
abstract: The Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect remains a cornerstone of fundamental and applied physics. In this work, we utilize the AB caging effect originated from an effective magnetic field induced by multi-orbital interactions, creating an all flat band (FB) lattice system. Normally, FB states are known for being compact in space and having a zero tail; therefore, their mobility in a linear environment is generally understood as impossible. We propose a Floquet driving protocol in an all-FB photonic system to fully control the dynamics of localized photonic states. The modulation of the Hamiltonian along the propagation coordinate allows the translation of compact states in the direction of constructive interference, resulting in an effective stroboscopic quantum walk-like effect. We find that the traveling states exist in chiral pairs and have a related topological invariant (winding number) equal to +1 or -1, with the sign determining the propagation direction. We experimentally implement the Floquet driven protocol using femtosecond laser written photonic waveguides and demonstrate directional control of the propagation, determined by the relative phase of the input condition.
summary: The research demonstrates how to overcome the inherent localization of compact topological photonic states by employing a Floquet engineering protocol in an engineered photonic lattice. By periodically modulating the system's Hamiltonian, the authors achieve directional transport, mimicking a stroboscopic quantum walk. This work is significant for realizing controllable light-matter interactions and robust information transfer in integrated optical circuits.
main_problem: The work addresses how to control the transport of highly localized, compact topological photonic states that are normally immobile in linear waveguides.
main_result: By applying a Floquet driving protocol—periodically modulating the lattice Hamiltonian—the authors successfully induce directional, quantum walk-like transport of these otherwise trapped states.
method: The study combines theoretical analysis using Floquet theory and topological invariants (winding number) with experimental implementation using femtosecond laser written photonic waveguides.
model_or_system: The system is an all-flat band (FB) lattice realized in a diamond structure connecting S-type and P-type waveguides, which mimics the effect of an effective magnetic field via multi-orbital interactions.
key_observables: Directional propagation confirmed by chiral pairs with winding numbers $\pm 1$, measurable discrete mobility ($D$), and low leakage fraction ($L$) during transport.
important_parameters: The control mechanism relies on modulating the Hamiltonian along the propagation coordinate ($z$) and controlling the relative phase of the input excitation.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include the ability to tune waveguide properties for matching band structures ($ eta_S =  eta_P$) and that transport can be achieved by swapping central waveguides periodically.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lattice structure, Bloch bands showing flat bands, the evolution of in-phase/out-of-phase states over one period, and experimental intensity profiles demonstrating clear directional wavepacket transfer across multiple mask segments.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using AB caging effects and FB states. It then details the Floquet driving protocol via periodic Hamiltonian modulation ($H(z)$). The core is the demonstration of controlled transport, culminating in experimental measurements of directional propagation and mobility.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete platform (photonic waveguides) to realize and control topological phenomena previously confined to theoretical models or other physical systems. It demonstrates active control over fundamentally localized quantum states using time-periodic driving, which is highly relevant for building optical quantum circuits.
